story_plain_checked: In Ryder's Book I, the jackal Victor tells this story to the bull Lively. He uses it to warn that you should not fight before you have measured your enemy's strength. A plover named Sprawl and his wife Constance live by the sea. When she is ready to lay eggs she asks him to find a spot. He says to lay them in the family home by the shore. She objects that the ocean's tide might reach the nest and carry the eggs away. He boasts that the ocean knows him and would never be his enemy. She also tells him the fable of the three fish. The ocean overhears all of this, thinks the plover's pride is like that of a bird holding up the sky with its claws, and decides to test him. The next day, while both plovers are out looking for food, the ocean reaches up with its waves and takes the eggs. Constance is heartbroken. Sprawl calls together all the birds. First they beat the water with their wings and try to fill the sea with dirt. Then, on an old gander's advice, they go to Garuda, king of the birds. Garuda refuses to go to Vishnu until the eggs are returned. Vishnu comes in person and orders the ocean, under threat of his fire-arrow, to give the eggs back. The frightened ocean returns them to the plover.
exact_quotes:
Arthur W. Ryder, The Panchatantra (University of Chicago Press, 1925), Book I 'The Loss of Friends', pp. 145-162. Checked against two separate archive.org scans, which agree.
(1) Names, p.145: "The plover was called Sprawl, and his wife's name was Constance."
(2) Wife, pp.145-146: "Here is the ocean near at hand. His tide might some day make a long reach and lick away my babies." (Ryder prints 'some day' as two words, not 'someday'.)
(3) Husband, p.146: "Sweetheart, he knows me, he knows Sprawl. Surely the great ocean cannot show such enmity to me." (Exact match.)
(4) The ocean's thought, p.151: "So Constance laid her eggs, but the ocean, who had listened to the previous conversation, thought: 'Well, well! There is sense in the saying: Of self-conceit all creatures show / An adequate supply: / The plover lies with claws upstretched / To prop the falling sky. / I will just put his power to the test.'"
(5) Taking the eggs, p.151: "So the next day, when the two plovers had gone foraging, he made a long reach with his wave-hands and eagerly seized the eggs."
(6) Ending, p.162: Vishnu says "Villain, give the plover his eggs. Else, I will reduce you to dry land." Then: "On hearing this, the ocean, while all his train shook with fright, tremblingly took the eggs and restored them to the plover, as the blesséd one directed."
(7) Frame verse that Victor says to Lively, p.145: "He loses fights who fights before / His foeman's power is reckoned: / The ocean and the plover fought, / And ocean came out second."
problems: Most claims check out. Corrections: (a) The quote reads 'some day' (two words) in Ryder, not 'someday'. (b) The names are right: the husband is Sprawl and the wife is Constance. (c) The 'claws upstretched' line belongs to the ocean, but it is a silent thought, not spoken aloud. The ocean is quoting an existing saying, which opens with 'Of self-conceit all creatures show / An adequate supply:'. Ryder uses the same verse again later in Book I, said by a monkey about a hen-sparrow, so it is not unique to the ocean. (d) The wife does not exactly 'want to move' at first. She asks her husband to find a spot to lay her eggs, he says to lay them here, and she objects because of the tide. Later she says 'I told you more than once that we should move.' (e) Between gathering the birds and going to Garuda, the claim skips two steps: the birds beat the ocean with their wings and try to fill it with dirt, and an old gander tells them to go to Garuda. (f) Vishnu does more than order the ocean: he fits a fire-arrow to his bow and threatens to turn it into dry land. (g) The story is told by the jackal Victor to the bull Lively. Its stated moral is about not fighting before you know your foe's power, and Sprawl is shown as a boaster. (h) Family-friendly note: after losing the eggs, Constance says something very dark about herself. Summarize it only as 'she is heartbroken'.

story_plain_checked: Constance, the hen-plover, tells this story to her husband Sprawl. She is warning him against his careless attitude toward the ocean. The whole story sits inside the plover tale, which Victor the jackal tells Lively the bull. Three grown fish named Forethought, Readywit and Fatalist live in a great lake. Forethought overhears passers-by and fishermen on the bank say there are plenty of fish here and that they will go fishing tomorrow. Forethought invites the other two to move with him to a safer lake. Readywit says he will think of something if the fishermen come, and Fatalist refuses to leave the lake he was born in because of mere gossip. So Forethought leaves alone. The next day the fishermen net every fish in the pool. Readywit plays dead and is laid on the bank, then wriggles back into the water. Fatalist struggles in the net and does not survive. Afterwards Sprawl asks his wife why she thinks he is like Fatalist.
exact_quotes:
Arthur W. Ryder, The Panchatantra (1925), Book I, pp.149-151. The tale's title is printed 'FORETHOUGHT, READYWIT, AND FATALIST'.
(1) Constance introduces the tale, p.149: "And Constance continued: Forethought and Readywit thrive; / Fatalist can't keep alive. 'How was that?' asked Sprawl. And she told the story of"
(2) Names, p.149: "In a great lake lived three full-grown fishes, whose names were Forethought, Readywit, and Fatalist."
(3) The warning, pp.149-150: "Forethought overheard passers-by on the bank and fishermen saying: 'There are plenty of fish in this pond. Tomorrow we go fishing.'"
(4) Forethought's reaction, p.150: "This looks bad. Tomorrow or the day after they will be sure to come here. I will take Readywit and Fatalist and move to another lake whose waters are not troubled."
(5) Readywit's escape, pp.150-151: "Readywit, while still in the water, played dead. And since they thought: 'This big fellow died without help,' they drew him from the net and laid him on the bank, from which he wriggled back to safety in the water."
(6) Closing verse, p.151: "'And that is why I say: Forethought and Readywit thrive; / Fatalist can't keep alive.'"
problems: (a) Spelling: in the title, the list of names, and both appearances of the verse, Ryder prints 'Readywit' as one word with no hyphen. 'Ready-Wit' and 'Ready-wit' are not his spelling. The verse should read exactly: 'Forethought and Readywit thrive; / Fatalist can't keep alive.' (b) The fishermen do not say 'we will come tomorrow'. They say 'There are plenty of fish in this pond. Tomorrow we go fishing.' It is Forethought who concludes they will come 'Tomorrow or the day after'. (c) Forethought does not leave 'at once'. He first invites the other two to come with him, and only leaves once they refuse. (d) Readywit escapes after he is already caught in the net with all the other fish. He plays dead, is laid on the bank, and wriggles back into the water. (e) The teller is Constance, the wife, speaking to Sprawl. It is a story within a story within Victor's tale to Lively. (f) Family-friendly note: describe Fatalist's end only as 'is caught and does not survive'. The text describes it with violence.

story_plain_checked: One morning Manu was given water for washing, and while he washed, a small fish came into his hands. The fish said, 'Rear me, I will save thee!' and told him a flood would come and carry away all creatures. It asked him to keep it first in a jar, then in a pit he would dig, and then to take it down to the sea once it had grown. It soon became a large fish and told him in which year the flood would come, and that he should prepare a ship. When the flood rose, Manu got into the ship, the fish swam up, and he tied the ship's rope to its horn; by that means he passed swiftly up to the northern mountain. The fish told him to fasten the ship to a tree and to come down gradually as the water went down, which he did. After the flood, Manu was the only one left.
exact_quotes:
Julius Eggeling, Satapatha-Brahmana Part 1, SBE vol. 12 (1882), Kanda I, Adhyaya 8, Brahmana 1, pp. 216-218 (checked against the 1882 scan OCR on archive.org and the wisdomlib transcription):
- Para 1: "When he was washing himself, a fish came into his hands."
- Para 2: "It spake to him the word, 'Rear me, I will save thee!' 'Wherefrom wilt thou save me?' 'A flood will carry away all these creatures: from that I will save thee!' 'How am I to rear thee?'"
- Para 3: "Thou wilt first keep me in a jar. When I outgrow that, thou wilt dig a pit and keep me in it. When I outgrow that, thou wilt take me down to the sea, for then I shall be beyond destruction."
- Para 4: "Thereupon it said, 'In such and such a year that flood will come. Thou shalt then attend to me (i.e. to my advice) by preparing a ship; and when the flood has risen thou shalt enter into the ship, and I will save thee from it.'"
- Para 5: "The fish then swam up to him, and to its horn he tied the rope of the ship, and by that means he passed swiftly up to yonder northern mountain."
- Para 6: "It then said, 'I have saved thee. Fasten the ship to a tree; but let not the water cut thee off, whilst thou art on the mountain. As the water subsides, thou mayest gradually descend!'" The quote in the claim matches the printed wording exactly, including the closing exclamation mark. It just leaves out the opening sentence "I have saved thee."
- Para 6 continues: "Accordingly he gradually descended, and hence that (slope) of the northern mountain is called 'Manu's descent.'"
source_url_checked: https://archive.org/download/wg912/WG912-1882%20-The%20Sacred%20Books%20of%20East%20-%20Vol%2012%20of%2050-Satapatha-Brahmana%20Part%201%20Of%205_djvu.txt (1882 SBE 12 scan OCR); https://www.wisdomlib.org/hinduism/book/satapatha-brahmana-english/d/doc63144.html. sacred-texts.com (sbe1234.htm) returned 403/Cloudflare and was NOT used.
problems: 1) Wrong word: Eggeling has 'dig a pit', not 'trench'. Change it to 'pit' (or 'a pit he dug'). 2) 'Tells him the year' is fine as a paraphrase, but the text only says 'In such and such a year that flood will come.' It never names an actual year. 3) In para 5 the subject is uncertain. Eggeling's footnote says 'he' could be 'it' (the ship or the fish), and Max Muller translates it as 'The fish carried him by it over the northern mountain.' So 'the fish takes him to the northern mountain' is a fair paraphrase, but it is not a literal quote. 4) The ship instruction is also uncertain. Eggeling marks 'attend to me ... by preparing a ship' as tentative, and Max Muller has 'Build a ship then, and worship me.' 5) Transcription error on wisdomlib: its page prints "Alarm's descent", but the 1882 scan reads "Manu's descent". If you need that phrase, use the scan's wording. 6) Family-friendly: para 3 has 'fish devours fish' and para 6 ends with the flood sweeping away all creatures. Keep these as neutral summaries ('the flood covered everything; only Manu remained') and don't quote them.

story_plain_checked: In Gita 2.40, Krishna says that on this path no effort is wasted and nothing goes against you, and that even a little of this dharma protects a person from great fear (Sanskrit 'svalpam apy asya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt'). Telang translates the last phrase as protection 'from great danger', and Arnold as being saved 'from the anguish of thy dread.' Gita 16.1 opens the list of godlike qualities, and the first word is 'abhayaṃ', fearlessness. Telang puts 'Freedom from fear' first and Arnold puts 'Fearlessness' first. Gita 18.30 says the sattvic (clear, good) understanding knows action and inaction, what should and should not be done, fear and freedom from fear ('bhayābhaye'), and bondage and liberation. Telang renders 'bhayābhaye' as 'danger and the absence of danger', and Arnold as 'What should be feared, and what should not be feared.'
exact_quotes:
SANSKRIT (GRETIL, Bhagavadgita with 4 commentaries):
- 2.40: "nehābhikrama-nāśo 'sti pratyavāyo na vidyate | svalpam apy asya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt ||40||"
- 16.1: "abhayaṃ sattva-saṃśuddhir jñāna-yoga-vyavasthitiḥ | dānaṃ damaś ca yajñaś ca svādhyāyas tapa ārjavam ||1||"
- 18.30: "pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca kāryākārye bhayābhaye | bandhaṃ mokṣaṃ ca yā vetti buddhiḥ sā pārtha sāttvikī ||30||"

TELANG, SBE vol. 8 (1882), 1882 scan OCR. Telang prints prose with no verse numbers, so each verse was matched to its passage by sense:
- 2.40 (p. 47): "In this (path to final emancipation) nothing that is commenced becomes abortive; no obstacles exist; and even a little of this (form of) piety protects one from great danger." Telang's footnote on 'great danger' reads: "Viz. this mortal mundane life."
- 16.1 (p. 114, start of Chapter XVI): "Freedom from fear, purity of heart, perseverance in (pursuit of) knowledge and abstraction of mind, gifts, self-restraint, and sacrifice, study of the Vedas, penance, straightforwardness," The list then runs on through 16.3 and ends: "(these), O descendant of Bharata! are his who is born to godlike endowments."
- 18.30 (p. 125): "That intelligence, O son of Pṛthā! is good which understands action and inaction, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, danger and the absence of danger, emancipation and bondage." The wording was also confirmed on wisdomlib, which spells the name Pṛthā.

ARNOLD, The Song Celestial (Trübner, 1885). Checked on the 1885 scan and on Project Gutenberg #2388; the words are identical, and Gutenberg prints dashes as '--':
- 2.40 (1885 ed. p. 17): "Here shall no end be hindered, no hope marred, / No loss be feared: faith—yea, a little faith— / Shall save thee from the anguish of thy dread."
- 16.1 (Chapter XVI, opening lines): "Fearlessness, singleness of soul, the will / Always to strive for wisdom; opened hand / And governed appetites; and piety, / And love of lonely study; humbleness, / Uprightness,"
- 18.30 (Chapter XVIII): "Good is the Intellect which comprehends / The coming forth and going back of life, / What must be done, and what must not be done, / What should be feared, and what should not be feared, / What binds and what emancipates the soul: / That is of Sattwan, Prince! of \"soothfastness.\""

XVIII); https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/2388/pg2388.txt (Arnold); https://archive.org/download/songcelestialor01arnogoog/songcelestialor01arnogoog_djvu.txt (Arnold, Trübner 1885 scan)
problems: Everything claimed about the Sanskrit is correct: 'svalpam apy asya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt' (2.40), 'abhayaṃ' as the first word of 16.1, and 'bhayābhaye' in 18.30. Cautions on wording: 1) Neither 1880s translation says 'great fear' in 2.40. Telang has 'protects one from great danger' (dharma = 'piety'), and Arnold has 'a little faith— / Shall save thee from the anguish of thy dread' (dharma = 'faith'). The literal Sanskrit is 'great fear', but do not put 'great fear' in quotation marks and credit it to Telang or Arnold. 'Practice/duty' is a modern gloss of dharma, so label it as a paraphrase. 2) In 18.30 Telang renders bhayābhaye as 'danger and the absence of danger'. The wording 'what is to be feared and what is not' is close to Arnold's, not Telang's. 3) 16.1 is only the start of the list, which runs through 16.3. Fearlessness comes first in the Sanskrit and in both translations, so the claim stands. 4) Telang gives no verse numbers; I matched the verses to his prose by sense, against the Sanskrit. 5) Minor OCR noise in the scans (for example 'piety.' where Gutenberg has 'piety,'). Where they differ I followed the Gutenberg/wisdomlib punctuation; the words themselves match the scans.
